sections.heading: What is the Top K Elements Pattern?
sections.content: This pattern finds the K largest, K smallest, K most frequent or K closest items in a collection without fully sorting it. The trick is to keep a heap (priority queue) of size K. Each new element is compared with the heap's top, so you only ever store K items. That gives O(n log k) time, which is much better than O(n log n) when K is small.

Keywords: top K, K-th, K closest, K frequent, K largest, K smallest
Full sorting is too slow or the data arrives as a stream

sections.heading: The Counter-Intuitive Rule
sections.content: To find the K largest, use a MIN heap. The smallest of your current K candidates sits on top, so when a bigger number arrives you remove that top and insert the new one. To find the K smallest, use a MAX heap for the same reason. Remember it as: the heap holds the winners and its top is the weakest winner.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Using a max heap for K largest (it should be a min heap) and vice versa
Forgetting to pop when the heap size goes above K
Putting the whole array in a heap and calling it O(n log k)
Subtracting values in a comparator, which can overflow (use compareBy or compareByDescending)
Forgetting that PriorityQueue iteration is not in sorted order; poll repeatedly or sort the result
Using remove(x) on PriorityQueue in a loop, which is O(n) each
Wrong tie-breaking when equal counts must be sorted alphabetically
Using sqrt for distance comparison; compare squared distances instead

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Keep a heap of size K instead of sorting everything
K largest uses a min heap, and K smallest uses a max heap
After each insert, remove the top when the size exceeds K
Time is O(n log k), which beats O(n log n) when K is small
For frequency problems, count with a HashMap first, then use a heap on the counts
Heaps also fit streaming data, since each new item costs only O(log k)
